blocks.p: A square matrix is **diagonal** if every entry off the main diagonal is zero; the diagonal entries can be anything, including zero, as in $\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix}$.
A **scalar** matrix is a diagonal matrix with every diagonal entry equal to the same number $k$, such as $5I = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$.

The **identity** matrix $I$ is the scalar matrix with $k = 1$. It behaves like 1 in multiplication: $AI = IA = A$. So every identity matrix is scalar and every scalar matrix is diagonal, but not the other way round.

The **zero** matrix $O$ has every entry 0. An **upper triangular** matrix has zeros below the diagonal, and a **lower triangular** one has zeros above it. A triangular matrix's determinant is the product of its diagonal: $\det\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = 2 \times (-3) \times 1 = -6$.

sections.heading: Worked example: how special matrices multiply

blocks.p: Diagonal matrices multiply entry by entry along the diagonal. A scalar matrix $kI$ commutes with every square matrix of the same order, $kI \cdot M = M \cdot kI = kM$, and $\det\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix} = -28$.

sections.heading: Worked example: using a stated property

blocks.p: If $\begin{bmatrix} x+2 & y-3 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}$ is a scalar matrix, the off-diagonal entry must be 0, so $y = 3$, and the diagonal entries must match, so $x + 2 = 4$ and $x = 2$.
If $\begin{vmatrix} 3 & x \\ x & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 4 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$, then $3 - x^2 = 3 - 8 = -5$, so $x^2 = 8$ and $x = \pm 2\sqrt2$.

list: **Calling any matrix with zeros on its diagonal a diagonal matrix.** It's the *off*-diagonal entries that must be zero.
**Assuming a diagonal matrix must be scalar.** Its diagonal entries can differ.
**Keeping only one root.** $x^2 = 8$ gives two values of $x$.
**Thinking only the identity commutes with everything.** Every scalar matrix $kI$ does.
